Literally
LIT-er-uh-lee
adverb (Millennial slang)
From Latin litteralis (of letters), English since the fifteenth century for "according to the letter," "exactly." Its use as a mere intensifier, meaning the opposite ("I literally died"), is old: Dickens, Mark Twain, and F. Scott Fitzgerald all have examples. But Millennial speech made it constant ("I literally can’t," "it was literally the best"), and in 2011–2013 dictionaries, including Merriam-Webster and the Oxford dictionaries, noted the informal intensifying sense, to widespread protest. The word now carries two nearly opposite meanings.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In Millennial speech literally usually means "really, really" and often means "figuratively": "I literally died laughing." Nobody died. The word that once meant "exactly, according to the letter" has been worn into an intensifier that can say the opposite of what it says. The Christian observation: this is more than a pedant’s complaint, because Christians are people of a Book and of plain speech. God’s words mean what they say: "Every word of God is pure" (Pro 30:5); "The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times" (Psa 12:6). The Lord Jesus prayed, "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth" (Joh 17:17). A people formed by a true Word ought to care that their own words are true. "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour" (Eph 4:25). The intensifier literally is not usually a lie, since no one is deceived, but it is a symptom of speech that has lost its moorings: if literally can mean figuratively, the young lose a tool for saying "this really happened." That tool matters when you are telling someone that Jesus literally rose from the dead. "For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mat 12:37). A father teaches his children to say "really" when they mean really and "literally" when they mean it, and to keep one word strong enough to carry the resurrection.

Webster 1828 Definition

An old adverb ("according to the letter") worn by Millennial overuse into an intensifier that can mean the opposite; a symptom of unmoored speech, whereas the Word of God is pure and true (Pro 30:5; Joh 17:17).

LITERALLY, adv. (Millennial intensifying use, 2000s–present; older informal use since the 18th–19th c.) Used for emphasis, often of something not literally true: "I literally died." Standard sense: exactly, according to the letter.

Webster (1828), root literally: LITERALLY, adverb 1. According to the primary and natural import of words; not figuratively. A man and his wife cannot be literally one flesh. 2. With close adherence to words; word by word. So wild and ungovernable a poet cannot be translated literally

Decode for parents: keep one word in your family’s vocabulary strong enough to say "this really happened."

Key Scripture

Pro 30:5 — "Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him."

Psa 12:6 — "The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times."

Joh 17:17 — "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth."

Eph 4:25 — "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another."

Mat 12:37 — "For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned."

Modern Corruption

Literally, worn into a mere intensifier, can now mean its opposite; the loss weakens a people of the Book who need words that say "this truly happened."

expand to see more

The corruption is semantic decay with real costs. When the word for "actually, exactly" comes to mean "very" or even "not actually," speech loses its ability to mark fact from figure. That matters most for the gospel, which is not a mood but a report of events: "that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day" (1Co 15:3-4). A generation that hears "literally" as hype hears the creed as hype too.

The recovery is careful speech, practised in small things. Christians should be known for meaning what they say, for saying what happened, and for using big words for big things. Teach children the difference between a figure of speech, which Scripture uses gloriously, and an exaggeration that blurs truth. Then, when they say Jesus literally rose, it will carry the weight of the word.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin littera (letter) → litteralis → English literal, literally (15th c., "exactly") → 18th–19th-c. intensifier → Millennial ubiquity → 2011–2013 dictionary recognition.

Latin littera — a letter of the alphabet; litteralis — of letters

15th c.: literally — according to the letter, exactly

18th–19th c.: informal intensifier (Dickens, Twain); 20th c.: Fitzgerald

2011–2013: dictionaries note the intensifying sense; public protest

Biblical anchor: every word of God is pure (Pro 30:5); thy word is truth (Joh 17:17)
